schrodinger.quote: Schrödinger (1926, in the 1928 English collection) wrote the wave equation for a particle of energy E in a potential V as div grad ψ + (8π²/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0, “the differential operations are to be understood with regard to the line element (3)”. In one dimension, for mass m: d²ψ/dx² + (8π²m/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0 (Condon & Morse 1929, p. 224).

oscillator.quote: Oscillator levels, Schrödinger eq. (25′), p. 31: “Eₙ = ((2n + 1)/2) hν₀; n = 0, 1, 2, 3, … Thus as quantum levels appear so-called “half-integral” multiples of the “quantum of energy” peculiar to the oscillator.”

box.quote: Box levels, Mott (1930) p. 59: “ν_n = hn²/8ml²” for an electron between walls a distance l apart, and p. 61: a vibration of frequency ν “describes the behaviour of an electron of energy hν” — so Eₙ = n²h²/8ml².

example.quote: (If the box is 1 cm. long, and the energy of the electron about 20 volts, the interval between successive energy levels is 3·2 × 10⁻⁷ volt.)

tunnel.quote: Gurney & Condon (1928): “If a ball be moving in a valley of potential energy and have not enough energy to get over a mountain on one side of the valley, it must certainly stay in the valley for all time, unless it acquire the deficiency in energy somehow. But this is not so on the quantum mechanics. It will always have a small but finite chance of slipping through the mountain and escaping from the valley.”

condonMorse.transmitted: The fraction transmitted is therefore 1/CC̄ and the fraction reflected is DD̄/CC̄.
condonMorse.resonance: the transmission probability is increased whenever ka = nπ, that is, whenever an integral number of half de Broglie wave lengths is contained in the distance a.
condonMorse.erratum: Eq. (68.5), for W < V, is printed with + before (k₀/k − k/k₀)²; substituting ik for k in (68.4), as the text says, gives a minus sign. Only the minus sign makes the transmission 1 for a barrier of zero width.

alpha.quote: “By varying this height through a small range we can obtain all periods of radioactive decay from a fraction of a second, through the 10⁹ years of uranium, to practical stability.”
